generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, group work is common, from running a study together to a shared practical report, and tutors watch the process closely. They know that research is collaborative, and that a psychologist who cannot listen, divide work fairly, or manage disagreement will struggle in a lab or a clinical team. The behaviours they assess, communication, listening, flexibility and accountability, are the ones your discipline runs on.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students are planning a group study, when a teammate proposes an unusual measure for the variable they are testing.

Tom hears the suggestion, says 'sure, whatever works', and returns to his own part of the design. The idea is neither built on nor questioned. Later Tom complains that the study design felt incoherent. He heard the teammate but did not listen, because nothing was done with the contribution. This is participation without collaboration.

Amara hears the same suggestion and asks two questions about how the measure would be scored and whether it is valid, then proposes folding part of it into the existing design. The teammate feels heard, and the design improves. When a later task slips because a member is unwell, Amara takes on the data coding rather than let the team stall. This is collaboration: listening turned into action, with accountability.

Both were in the meeting. Only Amara did the thing tutors are actually assessing.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, group work is assessed for its process because research itself is collaborative. You can now explain why tutors value the process, tell real listening apart from merely hearing, and name the behaviour a situation is calling for. The next lesson looks at what happens when a research team falls into conflict, and how to reflect on it.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that counts as listening rather than just hearing?

items.text: She asked how the measure would be scored and folded part of it into the design.
She nodded along and said the idea was fine before moving on.
She wrote the idea down to mention in her reflective account.
She waited politely until the teammate had finished speaking.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara acted on the idea, which is what turns hearing into listening.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID with the idea, not how politely she received it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Listening meant asking about the measure and building part of it into the design. Nodding, noting it down, or simply waiting are all closer to hearing.
